messages.author: 453ddfeccaf29bbb
messages.subject: Naive question on handling high-dimensional cov/precision matrices
parts:
Hi folks,

I am not accustomed to having to worry about numerical accuracy in my coding. However, I'm quickly realizing that I really should be.

I've learned about log_sum_exp trick, and I've been trying to compute things in log-space to avoid numerical underflow. (Any other general tips would be appreciated!)

My main question is: what do I need to know about high-dimensional symmetric matrices? I'd like to compute log determinants and the such. I'd also like to compute quadratic forms. (Presumably, there's a smart way to compute these without inverting the matrix?)

I'm seeing that Stan seems so use the LDLT Factor. Is this what I should read up on?

Thanks very much in advance,
Alp

P.S. This whole discussion began as I realized my algorithms were only stable until dimension = 5. I think this is because Eigen has closed-form implementations of things like determinants up to that dimension. (I may be wrong.) Because when I go to dimension = 6, I seem to lose a lot of numerical stability.

messages.author: 2a7f346506a3e9ff
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Naive question on handling high-dimensional cov/precision matrices
parts:
Hi Alp,

Yes, read up on Cholesky factorizations in particular, LDLT is mild generalization of Cholesky which sometimes has better stability.  Internally for things like multi_normal and multi_gp Stan is generally doing what is numerical best practice for log determinants, quadratic forms, etc so they're a good place to look for how to deal with things if you're writing C++ code.  If you have more specific questions definitely ask as, much like the log_sum_exp trick, some of these issues are not well explained or documented anywhere.

The Stan model API that is exposed to users for implementing these things themselves is somewhat limited and may be a bit less optimal both numerically and in terms of efficiency.  Part of that is simply due to a lack of time, although in most cases it's simply not trivial to expose certain types of functionality.  E.G., the LDLT factorization would be very hard to expose to users in an (autodiff) efficient way.

Cheers,
Marcus

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: Naive question on handling high-dimensional cov/precision matrices
parts:
If you are using a covariance matrix (or precision matrix) as a parameter in a model, then it is much better to reparameterize the model in terms of a Cholesky factor of a covariance matrix (or precision matrix). There are several Cholesky factorizations. The one I am referring to here is the lower-triangular matrix with strictly positive diagonal entries, denoted L, such that L * transpose(L) is equal to the covariance matrix (or precision matrix) of interest. This has as much numerical stability as anything in Stan. However, in most cases, substantive discussion of the model will involve the covariance matrix (or precision matrix) and thus in order to figure out your prior for L, you have to take your prior for the covariance matrix (or precision matrix) and multiply by a fairly simple Jacobian determinant.

If you are talking about a known covariance matrix or something internal that you tune in your algorithm, then it is slightly better to use the LDL' form of the Cholesky factorization, which expresses a covariance matrix in terms of L --- which is lower-triangular and has ones on its diagonal --- and D which is a diagonal matrix with strictly diagonal entries. This form is better for matrices that are singular or nearly singular because Eigen does pivoting to avoid dividing by (nearly) zero. So, really it is PLDL'P' where P is a permutation matrix and you may have to keep track of the P matrix. It isn't necessary to worry about the P matrix in some cases, like solving least squares problems.

The other matrix decompositions, such as QR, eigenvalues / vectors, etc. are either not as fast or not as stable as the Cholesky factorizations, so you wouldn't ordinarily need to use them.

Ben

There are lots of such "tricks" and I don't think we have
a list anywhere. Everything from using
log1p(x) instead of log(1 + x) for values of x near 0 to
making sure exp() doesn't overflow anywhere by pushing the
logs through with algebra, to preferring A \ B to inverse(A) * B.

- Bob

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Naive question on handling high-dimensional cov/precision matrices
parts:
The quadratic form can be cleaned up a bit,

LLT<MatrixXd> L = H.selfadjointView<Eigen::Lower>().ldlt();

Eigen::VectorXd y = L.solve(x);
quad = x.squaredNorm();

The trace is a tricker one and I’m surprised more people don’t write it out more efficiently. Calling trace will be O(N^{3}) because of the intermediate matrix multiplication, but you can actually do it in O(N^{2}). In components,

Tr[A . B] = \sum_{ij} A_{ij} B_{ji} = A_{i-} B_{-i}

In other words, the trace is the inner product of the ith row of A with the ith column of B (or the other way around, it doesn’t matter) summed over i.

messages.author: 2a7f346506a3e9ff
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Naive question on handling high-dimensional cov/precision matrices
parts:
On Wed, Sep 3, 2014 at 1:58 PM, Michael Betancourt <betan...@gmail.com> wrote:
The quadratic form can be cleaned up a bit,

LLT<MatrixXd> L = H.selfadjointView<Eigen::Lower>().ldlt();

Eigen::VectorXd y = L.solve(x);
quad = x.squaredNorm();

This won't work if you're using ldlt(), as you need to divide by the square root of the diagonals of D. I'm guessing you meant to call llt() given the type of L but in that case L.solve() isn't computing what you mean to compute.  You want L.matrixL().solve().  We don't have LLT implemented for autodiff right now, so that's not really an option if autodiff is needed.

If using LDLT and dividing by the square root of the diagonals, it will be faster for simple double/float based arithmetic, but will be slower for autodiff because the square roots and divisions will add extra variables to the autodiff stack.  For autodiff with LDLT the quadratic form as it's in Alps notes is about as good as it gets with our code right now.

The trace is a tricker one and I'm surprised more people don't write it out more efficiently.  Calling trace will be O(N^{3}) because of the intermediate matrix multiplication, but you can actually do it in O(N^{2}).  In components,

Tr[A . B] = \sum_{ij} A_{ij} B_{ji} = A_{i-} B_{-i}

In other words, the trace is the inner product of the ith row of A with the ith column of B (or the other way around, it doesn't matter) summed over i.

It is written explicitly in the case of the inverse wishart because A is the inverse of Sigma so the trace can't easily be computed as a dot product without computing A explicitly.  Numerically it's more stable to compute A . B and then take its trace and it's basically as efficient.

Cheers,
Marcus

messages.author: 2a7f346506a3e9ff
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Naive question on handling high-dimensional cov/precision matrices
parts:
The best solution there is probably to recognize that basically everything you want to compute using scalar * A can be computed using A and then rescaling it appropriately.  E.G., (scalar * A) \ b = (1.0/scalar) * (A \ b) or det(scalar * A) = scalar^N * det(A) where N is the size of A.

Alternatively, if you *really* need to update the LDLT, you simply need to rescale the entries of D but I don't know if Eigen's API allows this (matrixD() may be const) and I know for sure that the Stan wrapping of LDLT doesn't.

Cheers,
Marcus

On Sep 3, 2014, at 2:44 PM, Alp Kucukelbir <akucu...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Interesting. The subtleties are deep...
>
> Another related question:
>
> Let's say I have an LDLT decomposition of some matrix A.
>
> I want to compute scalar * A.
>
> Eigen doesn't appear to allow setting/adjusting the L and D matrices without re-computing everything.
>
> Is there a trick for this that I'm not seeing?
>
> Cheers,
> Alp
>
>
> On Sep 3, 2014, at 2:15 PM, Marcus Brubaker <marcus.a...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
>> On Wed, Sep 3, 2014 at 1:58 PM, Michael Betancourt <betan...@gmail.com> wrote:
>> The quadratic form can be cleaned up a bit,
>>
>> LLT<MatrixXd> L = H.selfadjointView<Eigen::Lower>().ldlt();
>>
>> Eigen::VectorXd y = L.solve(x);
>> quad = x.squaredNorm();
>>
>> This won't work if you're using ldlt(), as you need to divide by the square root of the diagonals of D. I'm guessing you meant to call llt() given the type of L but in that case L.solve() isn't computing what you mean to compute. You want L.matrixL().solve(). We don't have LLT implemented for autodiff right now, so that's not really an option if autodiff is needed.
>>
>> If using LDLT and dividing by the square root of the diagonals, it will be faster for simple double/float based arithmetic, but will be slower for autodiff because the square roots and divisions will add extra variables to the autodiff stack. For autodiff with LDLT the quadratic form as it's in Alps notes is about as good as it gets with our code right now.
>>
>>
>> The trace is a tricker one and I'm surprised more people don't write it out more efficiently. Calling trace will be O(N^{3}) because of the intermediate matrix multiplication, but you can actually do it in O(N^{2}). In components,
>>
>> Tr[A . B] = \sum_{ij} A_{ij} B_{ji} = A_{i-} B_{-i}
>>
>> In other words, the trace is the inner product of the ith row of A with the ith column of B (or the other way around, it doesn't matter) summed over i.
>>
>> It is written explicitly in the case of the inverse wishart because A is the inverse of Sigma so the trace can't easily be computed as a dot product without computing A explicitly. Numerically it's more stable to compute A . B and then take its trace and it's basically as efficient.
>>
>> Cheers,
>> Marcus
>>
>>

messages.author: 2a7f346506a3e9ff
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Naive question on handling high-dimensional cov/precision matrices
parts:
On Wed, Sep 3, 2014 at 3:12 PM, Alp Kucukelbir <akucu...@gmail.com> wrote:
Sorry. I should be clearer. (BTW: I appreciate all the help guys -- this is immensely useful.)

I have A_old at iteration t-1. It is in LDLT form.

I have computed it's gradient. Call it G. I have a closed-form expression for it.

I want to compute A_new at iteration t in LDLT form.

Currently, it seems like I need to do something like

A_new = LDLT<MatrixXd>(A_old.reconstructedMatrix() + G);

I guess what I'm asking is: there's no "trick" to avoid that LDLT, right?

That's right.  The only possible trick is if you somehow know that G is a rank one update, e.g., G = u u^T for some vector u.  In which case the LDLT factorization can be (relatively) cheaply updated.  However, for a general gradient this is unlikely to be the case.

Cheers,
Marcus

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Naive question on handling high-dimensional cov/precision matrices
parts:
On Wednesday, September 3, 2014 4:10:36 PM UTC-4, Marcus Brubaker wrote:
On Wed, Sep 3, 2014 at 3:12 PM, Alp Kucukelbir <akucu...@gmail.com> wrote:
Sorry. I should be clearer. (BTW: I appreciate all the help guys -- this is immensely useful.)

I have A_old at iteration t-1. It is in LDLT form.

I have computed it's gradient. Call it G. I have a closed-form expression for it.

I want to compute A_new at iteration t in LDLT form.

Currently, it seems like I need to do something like

A_new = LDLT<MatrixXd>(A_old.reconstructedMatrix() + G);

I guess what I'm asking is: there's no "trick" to avoid that LDLT, right?


That's right.  The only possible trick is if you somehow know that G is a rank one update, e.g., G = u u^T for some vector u.  In which case the LDLT factorization can be (relatively) cheaply updated.  However, for a general gradient this is unlikely to be the case.

Or a sequence of rank-one updates, which is still unlikely to be applicable. You don't want to call the reconstructedMatrix() method because that will literally do the multiplication. It is presumably worth the trouble to retain the matrix whose factorization is A_old and add G to that before factoring again.

Also, remember to keep track of the pivoting.

Ben

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Naive question on handling high-dimensional cov/precision matrices
parts:
On Wednesday, September 3, 2014 9:12:22 PM UTC-4, Alp Kucukelbir wrote:
Marcus: that makes sense. I came to a similar conclusion by looking at what Eigen offered for the LDLT class.

Ben: that's a really good point. However, I missed the subtlety about pivoting. Do I need to keep track of pivoting if I'm using "reconstrucedMatrix()" too?

The reconstructedMatrix method reverses the pivoting so that it reconstructs the original matrix. But you already have the original matrix, so there is no reason to use that method, which mostly exists for unit testing.

Ben
